title: Triple-Jointed Escape: Racing Langevin Diffusions Out of a Losing Streak
paper: 2607.20882v2 - An Eyring-Kramers Law for the Hypoelliptic Third-Order Langevin Diffusion
pitch: The paper derives the sharp Arrhenius exponential AND prefactor for mean escape time from a metastable well when noise cascades through a 3-level Hörmander chain (jerk -> acceleration -> velocity -> position) instead of hitting position directly -- and proves the cascaded ('hypoelliptic third-order') system has a strictly SMALLER prefactor than standard underdamped Langevin, i.e. it escapes faster despite the kick being 'further away' from the thing that's stuck. Build a single-page canvas demo: a double-well potential (think 'stuck in a bad streak' basin) with two balls simultaneously simulated via Euler-Maruyama -- one classic underdamped Langevin, one third-order hypoelliptic -- racing to escape the well, plus a live histogram of first-passage times overlaid with the paper's closed-form Kramers prefactor prediction. Let users drag the well depth/friction sliders and watch the theoretical vs empirical prefactor track in real time.
discussion_why: the counterintuitive 'noise from further away escapes faster' result maps directly onto tilt/variance debates in poker and sports betting bankroll management, and the live race + histogram makes an abstract stochastic-process claim visibly, arguably verifiable.

title: Regime-Escape Alarm: Kramers Law Meets Few-Shot Trend Detection
paper: 2607.20882v2 (Eyring-Kramers) x 2310.10500v2 (X-Trend few-shot trend-following)
pitch: X-Trend's paper shows a cross-attention few-shot model beats classic time-series momentum by 10x Sharpe and recovers from regime breaks (like COVID) twice as fast by matching new market windows against a context set of historical 'regimes.' Eyring-Kramers gives a closed-form law for how long a system stays trapped in a metastable state before flipping, driven by the curvature at the well bottom and the saddle it must cross. Fit a toy double-well potential to a rolling volatility/momentum signal per asset, use the Kramers formula to output an expected 'time-in-regime' with confidence bands, and pair it with an X-Trend-style attention layer that flags 'this regime shift looks like these N historical windows' -- a bankroll/streak alarm for systematic sports bettors and trend-following traders who currently eyeball moving averages.
discussion_why: directly speaks to the trading/betting-streak crowd's favorite argument -- 'is this a real regime shift or just variance' -- by putting a rigorous escape-time number on gut-feel streak calls.

title: Momentum in Range-Space: Nesterov-Accelerated Distributions
paper: 2607.23008v1 - Nesterov acceleration in optimizing over probability measures
pitch: The paper shows heavy-ball and Nesterov momentum can be lifted onto the Wasserstein-2 space of probability measures via a Hamiltonian formulation, achieving the same non-asymptotic accelerated convergence rates as Euclidean Nesterov, now proven for particle-based (i.e. finite-sample) representations of a distribution. Build a canvas demo where a cloud of particles represents a 'range' (a weighted distribution over hand-strength or bet-sizing) and two clouds race under (a) plain Wasserstein gradient flow vs (b) the paper's Nesterov-lifted flow toward a target distribution (e.g. a bimodal GTO-like mixture); show the accelerated cloud overshoot-and-correct (classic Nesterov oscillation) while converging in fewer steps, with a live Wasserstein-distance-vs-iteration plot for both.
discussion_why: poker players argue about how fast to 'converge' a range against a new opponent read, and literally watching momentum overshoot-then-correct in distribution space turns an abstract optimization-theory result into a visceral, arguable animation.

title: Untangle This Bet: the Squarefree Matrix Trick for Telling Knots Apart
paper: 2608.06372v1 - Squarefree Matrix Formulas for the CWR Invariant of Alternating Knots and Links
pitch: The paper's actual trick: attach a commuting variable to each vertex of a knot's Tait graph, take matrix traces, and keep only the squarefree terms to isolate simple cycles -- this gives closed-form formulas for the CWR_4 and CWR_5 invariant components (plus vanishing criteria tied to graph bipartiteness) for any alternating knot/link. Build a short explainer + tiny interactive companion: hardcode Tait-graph adjacency matrices for a handful of classic alternating knots/links (trefoil, figure-8, Hopf link, etc.), compute the squarefree trace live in-browser, and pose it as a bar-bet -- 'these two tangled loops of rope look identical, are they actually the same knot?' -- with the invariant giving a provable yes/no the eye can't.
discussion_why: less native to betting/poker but the 'provably untanglable bar bet' framing and the sheer 'wait, math can prove two knots are different without untying them' surprise still lands as a fun whimsy/games detour on a math-adjacent Discord.

title: Jewel Flood — the Flood-It level that turns NP-complete on you
paper: 2606.23837v1 Flood-It with Jewelry -- Characterizing the Game Complexity for Cograph Generalizations
pitch: The paper classifies 1024 graph classes for the single-player Flood-It game by which of ten 'jewel' subgraphs (extensions of P4, e.g. bull, gem, P5) are forbidden: free of bull+gem+P5 is polynomial-time solvable, while thin-spider graphs excluding eight specific jewels are NP-complete -- they nail 896/1024 classes. Build a single-page canvas toy: generate a small board's adjacency graph, run a live forbidden-subgraph scan against the paper's jewel list, and flip a badge between 'POLY-TIME SOLVABLE' (green, with the actual optimal-move count computed) and 'NP-COMPLETE ZONE' (red, solver disabled, 'good luck'). Let users drag nodes to add/remove edges and watch the badge flip in real time as they cross the complexity boundary -- a literal, clickable phase transition in game difficulty.
discussion_why: A puzzle that visibly snaps from 'solvable' to 'provably no shortcut exists' as you nudge one edge is a great 'wait, really?' math hook for the games crowd, though it's more math-nerd than betting-floor material.

title: Prove-you're-clean: zero-knowledge anti-RTA verification for poker and chess
paper: 2608.02774v1 Privacy-Preserving AI Verification via Minimal Information Disclosure
pitch: MID formalizes verification as three knobs -- evidence channel, collection policy, release transformation -- over physical measurements, and shows a Groth16 zk-SNARK linear-projection mechanism hits 'perfect held-out verification and zero measured collateral leakage' on 3 of 6 tasks (identity/hardware/compute-scale checks) with explicit privacy-utility frontiers on the rest. Pitch: a licensable verification layer for poker sites/chess.com-style platforms where a player's device proves 'my decision-time distribution and process list match a no-solver-assistance profile' via a zk circuit, without ever revealing the screen, process names, or timing trace itself -- exactly MID's 'authorized result only, zero collateral' guarantee. Tonight's demo: a toy snarkjs circuit that proves a decision-time sample falls inside a human-only reference distribution without revealing the sample, with a slider showing the real privacy-utility tradeoff curve from the paper.
discussion_why: Real-time-assistance and engine-cheating accusations are one of the most recurring flashpoints on poker/chess discords, and 'you can prove innocence without showing your screen' is a genuine surprise that people will immediately argue is either genius or gameable.

title: Edit Ledger: credit-assignment for betting-model tweaks
paper: 2608.23631v1 TRACE: Transition-Aware Residual Control for Multi-Objective Materials Discovery
pitch: TRACE fixes a real gap in agent-driven optimization: agents know which final candidates succeeded but not which specific edit caused the improvement, especially when one edit helps one objective and hurts another -- tracking parent-edit-child transitions and pooling their effects lifted macro hit-rate from 18.13% to 25.96% over the prior SOTA (LLEMA). Port the same transition-ledger idea to a toy sports/props model: every parameter tweak (line threshold, weighting, feature) is logged as a parent-child transition with observed effect on two competing objectives (hit rate vs. CLV/variance), the ledger ranks which edits are safe to reuse vs. which quietly regressed the other objective, rendered as a branching skill-tree UI. Directly useful for anyone iterating a props/spread model who currently just eyeballs 'did that last tweak help.'
discussion_why: Bettors are constantly arguing over which specific model tweak actually caused a hot/cold streak versus variance -- a tool that formally separates 'this edit helped' from 'you got lucky' is catnip for a decision-theory-minded betting crowd.

title: Overload-o-meter: an adaptive learner that scores how you explain +EV concepts
paper: 2608.17150v1 KnowSim: Evaluating Information Calibration in LLM Assistants with User Simulators that Learn
pitch: KnowSim's core move is a user simulator with an explicit knowledge state -- a graph of Information Units with prerequisite edges that update under learning-theory rules -- scored on three axes: Knowledge Gain, Delivery Calibration, and Cognitive Overload, validated against 705 real human-AI conversations where different models won at different knowledge levels. Build a client-side toy: a simulated 'poker student' with a small prerequisite graph (pot odds -> equity -> ICM -> GTO ranges), the user types explanations at each step, and the demo scores Knowledge Gain/Delivery Calibration/Cognitive Overload live using the same update rules, visualizing when you dumped GTO jargon on someone who hadn't learned pot odds yet.
discussion_why: Poker and sports-betting coaching communities constantly fight over 'you're overloading beginners with solver talk' vs 'dumbing it down too much' -- a meter that quantifies exactly that tradeoff on your own explanation is a fun mirror to hold up on a coaching-heavy discord.

title: CFMM Geometry Explorer: Sculpt an AMM Curve, Watch Arbitrage Iron It Flat
paper: 2308.08066 — The Geometry of Constant Function Market Makers
pitch: The paper's core result is that every constant-function market maker (CFMM) — Uniswap-style constant-product, StableSwap, concentrated-liquidity, LMSR prediction markets, whatever — reduces to a unique canonical trading function that is nondecreasing, concave, and homogeneous, connected to its portfolio-value function by conic duality. Build a single-file canvas toy: let the user drag control points to sculpt an arbitrary (possibly non-concave, kinked) trading-function curve for a 2-asset pool, then hit 'run arbitrageurs' and watch simulated arbitrage trades literally iron out any non-concave kinks into the canonical concave hull in real time, with the implied marginal price and portfolio value plotted alongside. Add a toggle that overlays a binary LMSR curve (the AMM behind prediction markets) on the same axes so users see that a Polymarket-style prediction market and a Uniswap pool are the same geometric object with different curve shapes.
discussion_why: Watching arbitrage physically flatten a bad curve into the 'correct' shape is a genuine wait-really moment, and the LMSR overlay turns it into a direct betting/prediction-market/decision-theory argument starter.

title: Menu-Pricer: Real-Time Differentiated-Demand Pricing for Prop/Parlay Menus
paper: 2602.05137 — Nested Pseudo-GMM Estimation of Demand for Differentiated Products
pitch: The paper shows a nested pseudo-GMM trick that swaps the order of GMM optimization and the BLP fixed-point inversion, making the market-share-to-mean-utility inversion closed-form and separable per product — so demand estimation over huge product catalogs scales far better than classic BLP, with efficiency gains growing faster than linearly in the number of products. Pitch a B2B pricing engine for sportsbooks/DFS/prediction markets that treats a player-prop or parlay menu as 'differentiated products' (the way economists treat cereal SKUs) and re-estimates cross-elasticities and reprices the whole menu in near real time after a lineup change or line move, instead of an overnight batch job — a natural extension of SharpLab-style odds/CLV infrastructure.
discussion_why: Treating your parlay menu like a grocery-store SKU catalog is a genuinely surprising econ framing that betting-minded people will want to argue about (and it's a real fit for the SharpLab quant-lab crowd).

title: Averageness Slider: Crowd-Replicate the Beauty-Math Paper Live
paper: 2602.13368 — The Influence of Width Ratios on Structural Beauty in Male Faces
pitch: The study morphs interocular distance relative to face width across 21 variants from low/medium/high baseline ratios and finds (via Bayesian analysis) that proportions closer to the population average are rated most attractive, not the extremes. Build a single-file toy: a procedurally warped canvas face mesh with a hidden ratio parameter, presented as pairwise A/B votes ('which is more attractive?'); every vote gets logged client-side and live-plotted as a histogram of win-rate vs width ratio, so a Discord channel voting together watches its own curve peak near the middle in real time instead of at either extreme — an informal live replication of the paper's finding.
discussion_why: Face-attractiveness debates are inherently high-engagement and relatable, and 'the crowd's votes literally plot a bell curve peaking at average' is a delightfully surprising, whimsical payoff for a betting/games-minded server.

title: Gauge-Cheat: Watch a Toy Neural Net Game Its Own Loss Function
paper: 2607.12501 — Gauge-Fixing the Forward-Forward Objective
pitch: The paper's diagnosis of Forward-Forward training (sum-of-squared-activations 'goodness') is that a layer can cut loss cheaply by just inflating weight magnitude rather than actually learning to separate real vs. fake data — a scale/'gauge' exploit; their fix is a scale-invariant whitened goodness derived from a likelihood-ratio account, which recovers 4-7 points of accuracy and closes 16-61% of the gap to backprop specifically because it removes the gauge-cheat, not just because it caps the inflation. Build a tiny in-browser toy: 2-3 trainable units on a 2D scatter of real vs. contrastive points, a live weight-norm gauge dial, and a toggle between vanilla goodness and whitened goodness — with vanilla on, watch the norm dial spin up while the decision boundary barely moves (loss drops via cheating); flip to whitened and watch the boundary snap to the actual separator instead.
discussion_why: 'The AI cheats its own scoring metric instead of learning' is an inherently discussable, slightly unsettling AI/decision-theory story, even if it's a softer fit for a betting-first crowd.

title: Volatility Flip: The Variance Simulator That Explains Why Bankroll Variance Is Sometimes Your Friend
paper: 2511.01905 - The impact of nonheritable variation in division rates on population growth across environments
pitch: The paper's real result (validated on Chlamydomonas mutation-accumulation experiments) is that non-heritable variability in individual division rates has opposite effects depending on the environment: it drags DOWN the population growth rate (dominant eigenvalue) when conditions are favorable, but BUFFERS the population against decline when conditions are stressful -- because growth compounds multiplicatively and Jensen's inequality punishes variance under growth but rewards it under decline. Build a single-file canvas demo: a slider for 'variance in individual rate' and a toggle for 'favorable vs stressful environment,' simulating a population of agents (or reframed as bettors with variable edge/stake) and plotting the population/bankroll trajectory live alongside the analytic log-growth curve. Users watch the exact same variance knob flip from harmful to protective as the environment flips -- which is precisely the arithmetic-vs-geometric-mean tension at the heart of Kelly criterion debates.
discussion_why: This is a disguised Kelly-criterion/volatility-drag demo -- 'high variance saves you when you're losing but kills you when you're winning' is exactly the kind of counterintuitive claim that starts a fight in a betting/poker Discord about staking strategy.

title: Reset or Grind: First-Passage Time Explorer for Run-and-Tumble Particles
paper: 2606.00560 - Velocity Resetting of Inertial Run-and-Tumble Particles in Non-Newtonian Media
pitch: The paper's claimed result is specific and surprising: for a run-and-tumble particle with inertial velocity resetting moving through shear-thickening media, there's an optimal resetting rate that minimizes the time to reach a target (a U-shaped first-passage-time curve); but in shear-thinning media, no such optimum exists -- you should never reset, just grind. Build a canvas sim where a particle random-walks/tumbles toward a target with a 'reset rate' slider and a 'medium type' toggle, running thousands of trials to live-histogram first-passage times and show the U-curve appear/disappear depending on medium. Frame it explicitly as a 'when should you reset your strategy vs keep grinding' toy -- directly analogous to stochastic-resetting search theory, which is already used to model foraging, algorithm restarts, and (informally) bankroll/tilt resets.
discussion_why: Stochastic resetting is a genuinely surprising physics result (sometimes quitting and restarting is provably faster, sometimes it's provably worse) that maps almost too cleanly onto 'should I cut my losses and reset my session/bankroll' arguments poker and sports-betting players have constantly.

title: Population-Context Line-Anomaly Detector
paper: 2603.05534 - In-batch Relational Features Enhance Precision in An Unsupervised Medical Anomaly Detection Task
pitch: The paper's actual result: augmenting a CNN autoencoder's latent space with in-batch relational context (via batch-wise hypergraph estimation + a shared-weight graph convolution layer, producing a 'population-aware embedding') lifted brain-MRI anomaly detection from baseline to 0.90 AUC-ROC (+5.7% absolute) and 0.78 AP (+16% absolute), with gains that scale with batch size -- i.e., judging an individual scan relative to a mini-batch of 'normal' peers beats judging it in isolation. Port the same trick to betting markets: instead of flagging a line as anomalous against a fixed statistical threshold, embed it jointly with a batch of comparable lines (same sport, market type, book tier) via the same autoencoder+graph-conv architecture, and score anomaly relative to that live peer context -- a plausible signal for mispricing, arbing, or fixing.
discussion_why: Repurposing a medical 'is this scan weird compared to its peers' trick into 'is this line weird compared to its peers' is a fun, slightly conspiratorial pitch (match-fixing/line-anomaly detection) that a sharp betting crowd will immediately want to poke holes in.

title: Chemistry Inside a Mirror Box: Can an Empty Cavity Change a Reaction Rate?
paper: 2605.31188 - Thermal chemical reactivity in Frenkel exciton-polariton cavities
pitch: The paper's actual claim, using a generalized Tavis-Cummings model with explicit polariton dispersion and molecule counting: putting molecules in a strongly-coupled optical microcavity measurably shifts their thermally-driven chemical reactivity, and the effect is biggest for small, dilute molecular ensembles, grows with Rabi splitting (coupling strength), and is more pronounced at low temperature. A short explainer builds up 'why would bouncing light between two mirrors change chemistry' from vacuum-field fluctuations to polariton dressed states, paired with one small interactive toy widget (sliders for molecule count / coupling strength / temperature driving a toy reaction-rate curve) to let viewers feel the parameter dependence the paper reports.
discussion_why: Genuinely wild physics ('a mirror box changes your chemistry') but it has no natural hook into betting/poker/sports -- scored low here on purpose since it's a general-science-audience piece, not a Discord-debate starter.

title: Rainbow Round-Robin
paper: 2608.06369 — A proof of Andersen's rainbow path conjecture for large n (math.CO)
pitch: The paper proves that for large n, every proper edge-coloring of the complete graph K_n contains a rainbow path visiting almost all n vertices (each color used at most once) — closing a decades-open conjecture and beating the prior n-O(sqrt(n) log n) record. The killer crossover: a proper edge-coloring of K_n is literally a round-robin sports schedule (each color class = one perfect-matching round). Build a single HTML/canvas app: pick n (say 6-24 teams/players), auto-generate the standard round-robin coloring, then animate a backtracking/greedy search live-highlighting a rainbow Hamiltonian-ish path through it. Add a 'break the conjecture' sandbox where users hand-draw colorings for small n and watch how hard it is to avoid a rainbow path as n grows. Frame it as 'can you build a season schedule where a team's sequence of opponents never repeats a round-color, touching almost every other team exactly once' — instantly legible to anyone who's run a league or poker rotation.
discussion_why: Turns an abstract Ramsey-flavored combinatorics proof into a literal fantasy-league/poker-rotation scheduling puzzle — concrete, arguable, and has a genuine 'wait, that's always possible?' surprise.

title: Bluff Gradient: The Learning-Speed Race
paper: 2607.22982 — Finite-Time Analysis of the Natural Policy Gradient in Finite-Horizon MDPs (math.OC)
pitch: The paper gives the first finite-time guarantees for exact NPG in finite-horizon MDPs: constant step size only gets sublinear O(H^2/t) convergence, but a specific increasing step-size schedule flips it to linear/geometric convergence O((1-1/theta)^t). Tabular NPG has a closed form (softmax multiplicative-weights update: policy(a|s) ∝ policy(a|s) * exp(eta * Q(a,s))), so it's exactly implementable client-side. Build a toy horizon-3/4 poker-style decision tree (bet/check/call vs a fixed opponent range) and race two learners side by side: constant-step NPG vs the paper's increasing-step schedule, plotting distance-to-optimal-policy per iteration on a log axis so users watch one curve bend (sublinear) and the other go dead straight (linear/exponential). A horizon slider shows the H^2 penalty blowing up iteration counts in real time.
discussion_why: Directly answers 'how many hands does an AI need to learn optimal bluffing,' and the punchline that just changing the step-size schedule mathematically guarantees exponentially faster learning is a genuine surprise for a decision-theory-literate poker crowd.

title: Cascade Radar: Markovian Hawkes for Bet-Flow Risk
paper: 2607.20838 — Long-memory Markov chains with power-law intensities (math.PR)
pitch: The paper builds a finite-dimensional nonlinear Markov chain whose event intensity follows a power law, proves it's Harris-recurrent/ergodic, and shows via the local Whittle estimator that it exhibits genuine long-memory behavior near the boundary of its stability region — matching classical (infinite-memory) Hawkes processes but staying cheap to filter online since the state is finite-dimensional. Pitch: a real-time risk module for sportsbooks/prop-trading desks that fits this model to live bet-arrival streams and flags when a market has drifted toward the 'near-instability' long-memory regime — i.e., a steam move or correlated bet cascade forming — versus normal Poisson-ish flow, something classical Hawkes MLE is too slow to do live. Prototype tonight as a simulate-and-visualize demo: generate self-exciting arrival bursts, run the Markov intensity filter, and show a live 'cascade score' gauge crossing into the danger zone.
discussion_why: Steam moves and bet cascades are exactly what sharp bettors argue about constantly, and 'a finite-memory Markov chain can fake infinite memory' is a legitimately surprising math result to drop on a betting Discord.

title: The Universe's Amnesia Clock
paper: 2607.07556 — Entanglement Asymmetry in Random Quantum Automata (cond-mat.stat-mech)
pitch: The paper measures 'entanglement asymmetry' (how far a subsystem's charge distribution is from symmetric) in random quantum cellular automata versus fully Haar-random circuits. Both eventually restore local U(1) symmetry, but for automata the timescale to do so depends on the initial state (it doesn't for Haar circuits) — because participation-entropy conservation and how uniformly charge sectors get explored are coupled, and asymmetry decay tracks subsystem coherence decay exactly. Script a short explainer: 'why does a quantum system remember how it started, even after it forgets everything else' — visualize charge sectors spreading unevenly across a 1D chain for different initial states, with a playful framing that the opening conditions of a system (like the seed stacks/hands at a poker table) can permanently set how fast information equalizes.
discussion_why: Genuinely cool quantum-info visual and a real 'wait, it remembers the initial state?' surprise, but the poker/betting tie is only an analogy, not a mechanism, so it lands more as whimsy than hard debate fuel.

title: Deck-Count Duel: Watch Q-Learning Race a Card Counter
paper: 2308.07329v1 [q-fin.TR] Variations on the Reinforcement Learning performance of Blackjack
pitch: Single self-contained HTML/JS page implementing tabular Q-learning for blackjack from scratch, with a slider for shoe size (1 deck up to 8 decks, or continuous-shuffle). A live chart shows the Q-learning agent's convergence rate to optimal strategy right next to a hard-coded basic-strategy + Hi-Lo counting bot grinding hands; as you drag the deck-count slider you watch both the RL convergence speed and the counter's house edge shift in real time -- directly reproducing the paper's core claim that shoe size materially changes both how fast an RL agent learns optimal play and how much edge a card counter actually realizes against the house.
discussion_why: Card counting and an AI learning to beat blackjack are both bread-and-butter gambling-Discord topics, and 'deck size secretly changes how fast you learn to win' is exactly the kind of casino-rules 'wait, really?' fact that starts an argument.

title: Contradiction Untangler: Preference-Graph Stat Arb
paper: 2310.08284v1 [q-fin.PM] Statistical arbitrage portfolio construction based on preference relations
pitch: Interactive demo generating a handful of synthetic random-walk price series, computing pairwise mean-reversion z-score signals for every pair, and drawing the resulting directed 'preference graph.' Toggle pairs on and off and watch naive independent pairs-trading create contradictions (told to be long AND short the same name at once), then hit 'resolve' to see the paper's preference-relation algorithm collapse them into one consistent portfolio. Sliders for number of securities included and transaction cost visually reproduce the paper's two headline claims: performance improves as more securities are added, and returns stay robust even at high transaction costs.
discussion_why: Watching a graph literally untangle contradictory long/short signals is a satisfying 'aha,' and quant/arb-minded bettors will instantly recognize it as the same headache as holding opposite bets at two different books.

title: Catch the Cheat: Live Memorization Radar
paper: 2607.12438v1 [stat.ML] Fisher Rank Inflation: A Spectral Signature of Memorization under Label Noise
pitch: Single HTML file using TensorFlow.js to train a tiny 2-layer classifier live in the browser on a synthetic 2D dataset, with a slider controlling what fraction of labels are corrupted. Each epoch it computes the per-example last-layer gradients, takes their SVD, and plots the effective rank over training time -- reproducing the paper's headline 'rank bump' during the memorization phase -- next to a scatter of points colored by gradient contribution, so you can watch corrupted points come to dominate the top contributors right at the rank peak, exactly as the paper reports (69-96% of top contributors being corrupted at peak, an inflation signal that precedes visible test-accuracy degradation).
discussion_why: It's a literal live spectral lie-detector for a neural net catching itself cheating -- viscerally cool to watch, though it's more an AI/ML hook than a betting or poker one for this crowd.

title: Incremental Upcoding Radar
paper: 2602.04092v2 [econ.EM] Time-to-Event Estimation with Unreliably Reported Events in Medicare Health Plan Payment + 2606.23655v1 [cs.DS] Dynamic estimation of slowly varying sequences
pitch: A toy library that pairs the econ.EM paper's upcoding-intensity time-to-event estimators (built to stay robust when reported events are unreliable/undercoded) with the cs.DS paper's warm-started sequential-approximation trick: since the paper shows you can reuse prior computations and hit a tighter O(sum of changes) cost bound with on-the-fly change detection instead of recomputing from scratch, apply that to rolling upcoding-intensity re-estimation across successive Medicare monitoring windows. Simulate a panel of enrollees with slowly drifting coding intensity (mirroring the econ.EM paper's own open-source R simulator), then show the wall-clock savings of warm-starting each period's estimate versus full recomputation, while still catching the same upcoding spikes the original estimator flags.
discussion_why: It's a step removed from betting/poker, but 'catch the party quietly gaming a scoring system for money' is the exact same instinct that drives sharp-vs-square and insurer-vs-sportsbook talk, just aimed at Medicare coding instead of odds.
